e.etymology: For boys, a Yiddish pet form of Mendel and Menachem, Hebrew for comforter, used chiefly in Hasidic families. Mendy has also been a girls' pet form of Melinda.
Two names share the spelling: for boys, a form of Arabic Adil, just or fair; for girls, a variant of Adele, from the Germanic element adal, noble.

assoc.t: Adele, the British singer (sounds the same)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Charlotte, the feminine of Carlos (Charles), which goes back to Germanic karl, free man. Empress Carlota of Mexico made it known in the Americas.
namesakes: Carlota of Mexico (Belgian-born empress of Mexico in the 1860s)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Qetsiah, cassia, a fragrant spice tree related to cinnamon. In the Bible, Kezia is the second of the three daughters born to Job after his trials.
The Slavic and Scandinavian spelling of Philip, from Greek Philippos: philos, loving, and hippos, horse. The name was borne by one of the twelve apostles and by the father of Alexander the Great.
Tied to the Dakota Sioux word koda, friend, the same root as the name Dakota; name books usually gloss it as friend to everyone. It came into use as an American first name in the 1990s.
The fictional village on Prince Edward Island in L. M. Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables (1908). The name reads as Avon, a Celtic word for river, plus lea, an old English word for meadow.

assoc.t: Avonlea, the village in Anne of Green Gables
Road to Avonlea, 1990s Canadian TV series

e.meaning: descendant of Raghu, a name of Rama
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Raghava, of the line of Raghu, a legendary king. It is one of the names of Rama, hero of the Ramayana, who belonged to that dynasty.
An English surname that began as a nickname from Middle English hert, a stag or male deer. The same spelling also anglicizes the Irish surname O hAirt.

assoc.t: hart, an old word for a male deer
comedian Kevin Hart
Hart Trophy, the NHL's most valuable player award

e.note: Sounds the same as heart, so the spelling often needs explaining.

e.etymology: An English surname from places called Penn, which keep the old Brythonic word penn, hilltop or head. It is also sometimes from pen, an enclosure.
namesakes: Penn Badgley (actor in Gossip Girl and You)

assoc.t: Penn, the University of Pennsylvania; also Penn State
William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania
actor Sean Penn
Penn tennis balls
Penn fishing reels

e.note: Sounds the same as the word pen.

e.etymology: From Basque arantza, thorn, and a short form of Arantzazu, the title of Our Lady of Arantzazu, whose image is said to have been found in a thornbush. Common in Mexico as well as Spain.
A modern American coinage that pairs the Jaz- of Jazmine and Jazlyn with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah and Janiyah. It has no meaning of its own.
A very short modern name in the family of Ila, Isla and Lily, also used as a pet form of longer names such as Iliana. It has no established meaning.

assoc.t: ILY, texting shorthand for I love you

e.note: ILY is everyday texting shorthand for I love you, and many people will read the name that way first.

e.etymology: A respelling of Kingston, an English place name and surname from Old English cyning, king, and tun, settlement. The -yn ending follows names like Jaxtyn and Brixtyn.

assoc.t: Kingston, capital of Jamaica, by sound

e.etymology: The French-style spelling, common in North Africa, of Arabic Yunus, the prophet Jonah. The name goes back to Hebrew Yonah, dove.
A recent respelling of Ellery, an English surname that goes back to the medieval given name Hilary, from Latin hilaris, cheerful. The -ie ending and the Ellie nickname give it a feminine turn.
A recent name in the mold of Leilani, Kailani and Milani, whose -lani ending is the Hawaiian word for sky or heaven. It has no established meaning of its own.
From Kandake, the hereditary title of the queens of Kush in ancient Sudan, which reached English through Greek and Latin. A Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, is mentioned in the Book of Acts.

assoc.t: Candace Flynn, big sister on Phineas and Ferb

e.note: Setup line of a crude internet joke (Do you know Candice?), so some teens will snicker at the name.

e.etymology: A spelling of Trey, the word for a three in cards and dice, from Old French treis. It began as a nickname for a boy who is the third of his name; tre is also Italian for three.
A pet form of David, from Hebrew Dawid, beloved, the name of the shepherd who became king of Israel. Davey has also been used on its own since the 1800s.

assoc.t: Davey of Davey and Goliath, claymation TV series
Davey Tree, national tree care company

e.etymology: A Scandinavian form of Nicholas, taken from the Latin church form Nicolai or the Russian Nikolai. All go back to Greek Nikolaos: nike, victory, and laos, people.
The Italian form of Victoria, from Latin victoria, victory, also the name of the Roman goddess of victory. It is the feminine of Vittorio.
From Arabic shakur, thankful or grateful; ash-Shakur, the Appreciative, is one of the names of God in Islam. US use as a first name rose after the death of rapper Tupac Shakur in 1996.

assoc.t: rapper Tupac Shakur

e.etymology: The Arabic and Turkish form of Aaron, the brother of Moses, who is honored as a prophet in Islam. It goes back to Hebrew Aharon, whose meaning is not known for certain.
namesakes: Harun al-Rashid (caliph of the Arabian Nights era)

e.etymology: A modern blend of Wesley and the -lyn ending of Evelyn and Brooklyn. Wesley is an English surname and place name meaning west meadow.
From Sanskrit mihira, the sun, a word related to the Persian Mihr and the ancient deity Mithra. Mihira is the feminine counterpart of the boys' name Mihir.
A modern American coinage with no known source word. It is best known as the birth name of rapper Lil Uzi Vert, Symere Woods, and its rise follows his fame.
A double-B spelling of Abigail, from Hebrew Avigayil, my father is joy. In the Bible, Abigail is the wise and quick-thinking wife of King David.
A clipped form of Jessica, spelled with a final i. Shakespeare introduced Jessica in The Merchant of Venice, probably basing it on the Biblical Hebrew name Iscah.
In Albanian, Era is a popular girls' name from era, the wind. In the US it was in use around 1900, and it matches the English word era, an age or period, from Latin aera.

assoc.t: era, the English word for a period of history
ERA, baseball's earned run average
ERA, the proposed Equal Rights Amendment
Era laundry detergent

e.etymology: A Vietnamese name given to both girls and boys, most often the Sino-Vietnamese reading of the Chinese character for peace and safety. The same character gives the Chinese name An.
e.note: Looks like the English word an, so it can get lost or misread in forms and plain text.

e.etymology: From Persian kam, wish or desire, with the suffix -ran: one whose wishes are fulfilled, so fortunate or prosperous. Used across Iran, Azerbaijan and South Asia.
